summary.text: Above the stated thresholds, any witness counted by the hypothesis immediately yields a Goldbach decomposition for even inputs and a Lemoine decomposition for odd inputs; exhaustive primality searches handle all smaller admissible inputs. If cousin-prime starts were bounded by \(M\), applying the hypothesis to the large even number \(16028M!\) would produce such a prime \(q\le M\), forcing \(q\mid M!\) and hence \(q\mid(16028M!-q)\), impossible because the latter is a strictly larger prime.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(n)=1+(n\bmod 2).
\]
Thus \(c(n)=1\) when \(n\) is even and \(c(n)=2\) when \(n\) is odd. The number \(a(n)=A219055(n)\) is the number of natural numbers \(q<n\) such that
\[
 (c(n)+1)q<n,
\]
\(q\) and \(q+6\) are prime, and
\[
 p:=n-c(n)q\quad\hbox{and}\quad p-6=n-c(n)q-6
\]
are prime. The inequality \((c(n)+1)q<n\) ensures that the subtraction defining \(p\) is an ordinary nonnegative subtraction and, moreover,
\[
 p=n-c(n)q>q.
\]
Consequently these are exactly representations
\[
 n=p+q\frac{3-(-1)^n}{2}
\]
with \(p>q\) and \(p,q,p-6,q+6\) all prime.

Assume throughout the core conjecture:

* if \(n>8012\) is even, then \(a(n)>0\);
* if \(n>15727\) is odd, then \(a(n)>0\).

We prove in turn Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture, and the infinitude of prime pairs \((p,p+6)\).

## 1. The finite computations below the two thresholds

We first describe the finite computations used for the integers not covered by the hypothesis. This also explains why those computations rigorously produce the required representations.

### Primality test

For an integer \(N\), primality was tested as follows.

1. If \(N<2\), declare it composite.
2. If \(N\) is even, declare it prime exactly when \(N=2\).
3. If \(N\) is odd, test successively the odd integers
   \[
   3,5,7,\ldots
   \]
   for divisibility into \(N\). If one divides \(N\), declare \(N\) composite. If the current candidate \(k\) satisfies \(N<k^2\) before a divisor has been found, declare \(N\) prime.

This is an exact primality test. Indeed, an odd composite number has a prime divisor at most its square root; that divisor is odd and is therefore encountered in the scan. Conversely, if no integer from \(2\) through \(\sqrt N\) divides \(N\), then \(N\) cannot factor as a product of two integers greater than \(1\), since in any such factorization at least one factor is at most \(\sqrt N\). Thus the test returns “prime” exactly for primes.

In the actual finite recursion, the odd-divisor scan was given \(N\) steps. This is more than enough: the candidates increase by \(2\), and the scan stops once they pass \(\sqrt N\). More explicitly, if a scan beginning at an odd candidate \(k\) has enough remaining steps to reach beyond \(\sqrt N\), then it gives the same answer as unrestricted trial division. Since \(\sqrt N\leq N\), a budget of \(N\) steps certainly suffices.

### Goldbach search

For a fixed \(N\), inspect candidates \(q=2,3,4,\ldots\), stopping before \(q=N\). At each candidate, apply the primality test to \(q\) and \(N-q\). The search succeeds as soon as both are prime. A successful search therefore explicitly supplies
\[
 N=(N-q)+q
\]
with both summands prime.

One can formulate this as the following finite recursion. A search with zero remaining steps fails. With at least one step remaining, it fails if \(q\geq N\); it succeeds if \(q\) and \(N-q\) are prime; otherwise it continues at \(q+1\) with one fewer step. Induction on the number of remaining steps proves that whenever this recursion reports success, it supplies a Goldbach representation. The computation for \(N\) starts at \(q=2\) with \(N\) available steps, so it has ample range.

Applying that search to every even \(N\) satisfying
\[
 4\leq N<8013
\]
gives success in every case. Equivalently, the exhaustive range computation on \([0,8013)\), ignoring numbers that are not even or are below \(4\), returns success.

The range computation itself can be viewed recursively: to check an interval \([s,s+L)\), first check its last member \(s+L-1\) if that member has the required parity and lower bound, and then check \([s,s+L-1)\). An induction on \(L\) shows that success of the whole range check implies success for every relevant integer in the interval. The direct exhaustive computation yielded
\[
 \boxed{\text{every even }N\text{ with }4\leq N<8013
        \text{ is a sum of two primes}.}
\]

### Lemoine search

For a fixed \(N\), inspect candidates \(q=2,3,4,\ldots\) while \(2q<N\). At each candidate, test \(q\) and \(N-2q\) for primality. A successful candidate gives
\[
 N=(N-2q)+2q,
\]
with both \(q\) and \(N-2q\) prime.

Again, the soundness is immediate by induction on the number of search steps: a report of success can occur only at a candidate for which both indicated numbers have passed the exact primality test. The computation starts with \(q=2\) and uses \(\lfloor N/2\rfloor\) steps, which is enough to inspect the entire potentially relevant range.

This search was exhaustively run on the odd integers at least \(7\) in the following four adjacent intervals:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{interval}&\text{outcome}\\ \hline
[0,4000)&\text{all relevant integers succeed},\\
[4000,8000)&\text{all relevant integers succeed},\\
[8000,12000)&\text{all relevant integers succeed},\\
[12000,15728)&\text{all relevant integers succeed}.
\end{array}
\]
As with the Goldbach check, induction on the interval length proves that a successful interval computation supplies a successful individual search for every relevant member. Since the four intervals cover \([0,15728)\), the computation establishes
\[
 \boxed{\text{every odd }N\text{ with }7\leq N<15728
        \text{ has the form }N=p+2q\text{ with }p,q\text{ prime}.}
\]

These are the only finite computations needed in the proof.

## 2. Goldbach's conjecture

Let \(n\geq4\) be even. We must find primes \(p,q\) such that \(n=p+q\).

There are two cases.

### Case 1: \(n>8012\)

By the core conjecture, \(a(n)>0\). Hence there is at least one \(q\) counted by \(a(n)\). Since \(n\) is even, \(c(n)=1\), so this \(q\) satisfies
\[
 2q<n,
\]
\(q\) is prime, and
\[
 p=n-q
\]
is prime. The inequality \(2q<n\) in particular gives \(q<n\), so there is no issue with subtraction, and
\[
 n=(n-q)+q=p+q.
\]
Thus \(n\) is a sum of two primes. Notice that the additional facts that \(q+6\) and \(p-6\) are prime are stronger than needed here.

### Case 2: \(n\leq8012\)

Then \(n<8013\). The finite Goldbach computation above applies and gives primes \(p,q\) with \(n=p+q\).

This proves Goldbach's conjecture for every even \(n\geq4\).

## 3. Lemoine's conjecture

Let \(n\geq7\) be odd. We must find primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
 n=p+2q.
\]
Again there are two cases.

### Case 1: \(n>15727\)

By the core conjecture, \(a(n)>0\), so choose a \(q\) counted by \(a(n)\). Since \(n\) is odd, \(c(n)=2\). Therefore
\[
 3q<n,
\]
\(q\) is prime, and
\[
 p=n-2q
\]
is prime. In particular \(2q<n\), and hence subtraction is exact and
\[
 n=(n-2q)+2q=p+2q.
\]
This is the desired Lemoine representation.

### Case 2: \(n\leq15727\)

Then \(n<15728\). Exactly one of the following alternatives holds:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&n<4000,\\
&4000\leq n<8000,\\
&8000\leq n<12000,\\
&12000\leq n<15728.
\end{aligned}
\]
The corresponding one of the four finite Lemoine computations supplies primes \(p,q\) with \(n=p+2q\).

Thus Lemoine's conjecture holds for every odd \(n\geq7\).

## 4. Infinitely many prime pairs differing by six

Let
\[
 S=\{q\in\mathbb N:q\text{ is prime and }q+6\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
We prove that \(S\) is infinite.

Suppose for contradiction that \(S\) is finite. A finite set of natural numbers is bounded above, so choose \(M\) such that
\[
 q\leq M\qquad\text{for every }q\in S.
\]
Define
\[
 N=16028\,M!=2\cdot8014\,M!.
\]
The number \(N\) is even. Also \(M!\geq1\), so
\[
 N\geq16028>8012.
\]
The even part of the core conjecture therefore gives \(a(N)>0\). Choose a number \(q\) counted by \(a(N)\). For even \(N\), the defining conditions say in particular that
\[
 q\text{ and }q+6\text{ are prime},
 \qquad p:=N-q\text{ is prime}.
\]
Thus \(q\in S\), and the choice of \(M\) gives \(q\leq M\).

Because \(q\) is prime, \(q>0\). Every positive integer at most \(M\) divides \(M!\), so
\[
 q\mid M!.
\]
Consequently \(q\mid N=16028M!\). Since of course \(q\mid q\), it follows that
\[
 q\mid N-q=p.
\]

We now show that this is impossible because \(q\) is a proper nontrivial divisor of the prime \(p\). First, \(q\geq2\), since \(q\) is prime. Next, from \(q\leq M\) and \(q>0\), the divisibility \(q\mid M!\) also gives \(q\leq M!\). Hence
\[
 N=16028M!\geq16028q,
\]
and in particular
\[
 p=N-q>q.
\]
Thus
\[
 2\leq q<p\quad\text{and}\quad q\mid p.
\]
But a prime number has no positive divisors other than \(1\) and itself. Since \(p\) is prime, \(q\mid p\) would force \(q=1\) or \(q=p\), contradicting respectively \(q\geq2\) and \(q<p\).

This contradiction shows that \(S\) cannot be finite. Therefore there are infinitely many primes \(q\) for which \(q+6\) is also prime.

Combining Sections 2, 3, and 4, the assumed positivity of \(A219055(n)\) for every even \(n>8012\) and every odd \(n>15727\) implies Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture, and the infinitude of prime pairs \((p,p+6)\), as claimed.
